title: Everything Is a Wave
reflection: When a strong feeling or thought arrives, ask three quick things: what kind of wave is this, how big and how fast is it, and is it pulling with me or scattering me? You are reading the wave as a wave.

questions.q: What does the word vṛtti mean, and what is the claim made about it?
o: A wave-formation that rises, holds and subsides in the mind: every thought, perception, memory and mood is a vṛtti.
A fixed trait of character that a person has from birth: anxiety and depression are examples of a vṛtti.
A stage in a person’s spiritual development that is reached with practice: a person moves up through each vṛtti.
A teacher who guides a pupil from outside: the vṛtti is the voice that gives advice and corrects mistakes.
questions.e: It comes from a root meaning to turn or whirl. Even the tree you see is, as you experience it, a wave your mind has formed. Dr Watson says a patient who says I am depressed has nowhere to stand, while one who says a wave of heaviness is moving through me has a foothold.
questions.c: Everything in experience is a vṛtti

questions.q: James says that stilling the mind is about letting the water settle so the bottom shows through. Which picture of Vivekananda does this follow?
o: A lake: the bottom is the deepest Self, the water is the mind, and the surface waves are the vṛttis.
A river: the source is the deepest Self, the banks are the mind, and the current is the vṛttis.
A mirror: the glass is the deepest Self, the frame is the mind, and the reflections are the vṛttis.
A fire: the flame is the deepest Self, the wood is the mind, and the smoke is made of the vṛttis.
questions.e: When the surface is whipped into ripples you cannot see the bottom, which was never disturbed. You do not beat the lake calm; the wind drops and it settles on its own. Patañjali’s definition of yoga is the settling of the waves of the mind.
questions.c: Settle the water, do not flatten the waves

questions.q: “A wave of anger or grief leaves a stain on the deepest Self, which is behind the waves and must defend itself against them.”
questions.e: The wave is not a foreign thing on the water; it is the water taking a shape for a moment, and when it subsides there is no residue. A vṛtti is awareness itself taking a shape and releasing it. The deepest Self is the very water the waves are made of, never harmed by them.
questions.c: Waves leave no stain on the water

questions.q: Kai hears a chord as one rich sound; a tuning app shows three pitches. What does Swamiji say about the two descriptions?
o: Both are true: one is the experience as it flows in time, the other the same sound as a set of frequencies.
Only the first is true, since a chord is a single sound and its notes are an invention of musicians.
Only the second is true, since the single sound is an illusion and the three pitches are what is real.
Neither is true, since a chord is a matter of taste and no description of it can be right or wrong.
questions.e: Nothing is left out of either. Ordinary mind lives in the melody, moment after moment; the deepest Self that the traditions point to is described from the second side, whole and timeless, like the chord. Kai says it is the first timeless Self line that has not made him wince, because he can check it with a chord.
questions.c: A chord has two complete descriptions

questions.q: Which three dials does Swamiji say describe any wave of the mind?
o: Size, speed and alignment: how vivid, how fast, and whether the waves pull the same way.
Height, depth and width: how tall the wave is, how deep it goes and how far it spreads.
Past, present and future: where the wave began, where it is now and where it is likely to go.
Light, sound and touch: which sense the wave arrives by, and how strongly that sense is felt.
questions.e: Size was met last module as the volume knob; speed separates a racing, fluttering mind from a slow, heavy one; alignment is whether thoughts, feelings, body and intentions are in step: sattva when aligned, rajas when scattered and churning, tamas when dull and flat.

questions.q: Dr Watson has two anxious patients: one buzzing and unable to sit still, one frozen and grey. How does Swamiji read them?
o: Same word, different settings: large fast waves in one, slow flat waves in the other, so different dials.
Same word, same settings: both are anxious in the same way, so one treatment will suit them both.
Different words, same settings: one is anxious and the other depressed, so the dials cannot be used.
Different words, different causes: the first is a fault of the body and the second a fault of the mind.
questions.e: Dr Watson says this is a diagnostic language: not just you have anxiety but right now your waves are large, fast and scattered, and here is which dial to turn first. A fact cannot be turned; a dial can. You are not fixing a broken person but learning the controls of an instrument.
questions.c: Read the dials, not just the word

questions.q: In the lesson’s account of who turns the dials, which worker mainly sets the speed of a wave?
o: Manas, attention, by how steadily the wave keeps its rhythm.
The body and prāṇa, by the energy and arousal behind the wave.
Buddhi, clarity, together with ahaṁkāra’s standing tilt, by the alignment.
Chitta, memory, by how long the stored impressions keep the wave ringing.
questions.e: The body and prāṇa mostly set the size; manas sets the speed; ahaṁkāra’s tilt and buddhi’s clarity together govern alignment; chitta is the field where the wave is recorded and shapes how long it rings. A vṛtti is made by the whole inner instrument.

questions.q: A person feels sure that everyone in a meeting was judging them, though nobody said a word. Which of the five kinds of wave is this?
o: Misperception: a vivid, convincing wave that does not match what is there, like the rope taken for a snake.
Clear knowing: the wave matches what is real, as when you see a cup and there is a cup.
Imagination: a wave with nothing outside it, such as a daydream, a plan or a poem.
Memory: a wave that revives an impression from the past and plays it back as it was.
questions.e: The five are clear knowing, misperception, imagination, sleep and memory. The cruelty of misperception is that it feels exactly as real as accurate knowing: the pounding heart at the rope is the same as at a real snake. That is why people cannot just think their way out.
questions.c: Misperception feels as real as knowing

questions.q: “Memory is playback: each time you remember, you press play on a recording, so it is always accurate.”
questions.e: Each time you remember you build a fresh wave coloured by today’s mood, so you furnish the same room differently when happy and when low. Memory is a present-tense painting using pigments from the past, which is hopeful: a painful memory is re-painted each time and can be re-painted more gently.

questions.q: Sarah’s worry about her children rises. What does the practical experiment ask her to do before acting?
o: Name it as an imagination wave about a future that has not happened, and notice if it loses some grip.
Argue with it until it is shown to be false, and then act only when the worry has been put right.
Ignore it entirely, since naming a wave only gives it more attention and makes it larger.
Act on it at once, since a wave of worry is a sign that something needs doing straight away.
questions.e: Recognition is not arguing with the wave but naming its kind: the instant you can, you are no longer fully inside it. James is to catch “they’re all bored of me” as a misperception-wave and look for the evidence; Kai to name the craving-wave and the flat-wave after scrolling without obeying them.
questions.c: Name the kind, then the size
